## Summary

- `KVCacheManager` is the scheduler-facing manager and instantiates a coordinator from the cache configuration. [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py:131-180]()
- `KVCacheCoordinator` constructs a shared `BlockPool` and creates type-specific managers for cache groups. [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:119-125](), [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:157-167]()
- `BlockPool` manages physical GPU blocks, eviction queues, and `BlockHashToBlockMap` prefix cache lookups. [vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:38-169]()
- Prefix identity uses `BlockHash` and group-qualified `BlockHashWithGroupId` keys; `init_none_hash` controls root seed reproducibility. [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:44-79](), [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:150-163]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py:131-180](), [vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:38-169](), [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:119-167](), [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:44-79](), [vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:150-163]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page describes how vLLM prepares requests for the engine and turns engine outputs into user-facing results. It covers the `InputProcessor`, renderer configuration and prompt handling, per-request output state, logprob data representation, and asynchronous collection of streamed responses [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:53-93]().

The input path connects prompt parsing and rendering to `EngineCoreRequest` construction; the output path processes engine outputs into completion or pooling results and makes those results available to consuming tasks [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:14-44]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:14-93]()

---

## Input Rendering and Multimodal Preprocessing

Input processing turns user prompts into engine-facing representations. `InputProcessor` owns the active renderer and model-related configuration, while the renderer handles prompt operations such as tokenization and multimodal preprocessing [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-172]().

### `InputProcessor`

`InputProcessor` is initialized with a `VllmConfig`, an optional `BaseRenderer`, and a multimodal registry. It retains configuration objects used during admission and validation, including model, cache, LoRA, scheduler, speculative decoding, structured outputs, observability, and diffusion configuration [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:170-172]().

If no renderer is supplied, `InputProcessor` obtains one through `renderer_from_config`. It exposes the renderer’s tokenizer and provides asynchronous wrappers around input processing using the renderer’s executor so blocking preprocessing does not run directly on the caller’s event loop [vllm/renderers/base.py:140-172]().

### Renderer Classes and Configuration

`BaseRenderer` is the abstract renderer base. It stores the vLLM and model configuration, API process rank, and tokenizer; it also manages cleanup resources and executor-backed operations [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-119]().

The base renderer uses a configurable thread pool for blocking tokenizer work and a separate single-worker executor for multimodal processing. It wraps tokenization, decoding, multimodal processing, cache clearing, and prompt-embedding loading in asynchronous helpers [vllm/renderers/base.py:140-172]().

`ChatParams` controls chat formatting and multimodal preparation options. Its fields include the chat template, content format, template kwargs, media I/O kwargs, multimodal processor kwargs, tool choice, and response format [vllm/renderers/params.py:93-116](). `with_defaults` combines request values with defaults, and `get_apply_chat_template_kwargs` builds the arguments for applying a tokenizer chat template [vllm/renderers/params.py:117-155]().

`TokenizeParams` configures tokenization limits and transformations. Its documented fields include total and output token limits, padding and truncation controls, truncation side, lowercasing, special-token behavior, optional character-offset return, and whether the prompt must retain its original text for later detokenization [vllm/renderers/params.py:158-208]().

### Input Data Flow

Diagram: Prompt admission from user input to engine request
```mermaid
graph LR
    UserPrompt["UserPrompt"] --> ParsePrompt["parse_model_prompt"]
    ParsePrompt --> InputProcessor["InputProcessor"]
    InputProcessor --> Renderer["BaseRenderer"]
    Renderer --> Tokenize["TokenizationAndPreprocessing"]
    Tokenize --> EngineRequest["EngineCoreRequest"]
```

The diagram maps user-facing prompt concepts to the code entities visible in the input processor and renderer imports. `InputProcessor` creates or accepts a renderer, and the input-processing module imports both prompt parsing and request classes [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-172](), [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:170-172]().

Sources: [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-172](), [vllm/renderers/params.py:93-208](), [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:170-172]()

---

## Output Processing and Detokenization

The output-processing subsystem maintains request-local state and converts engine results into public response objects. The output processor module imports `IncrementalDetokenizer` and `LogprobsProcessor`, and its request state holds references to both when supplied [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-44](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:183-197]().

### `RequestState`

`RequestState` is initialized with request identifiers, parallel-sampling metadata, LoRA information, output kind, prompt data, a logprobs processor, a detokenizer, and token limit parameters [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:183-197](). These fields provide request-local context for producing outputs.

### Incremental Detokenization

`OutputProcessor` uses `IncrementalDetokenizer` as a per-request output component, and output-processing tests exercise incremental decoding over successive engine outputs for both delta and final-only output kinds [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-35](), [tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py:124-179]().

The tests also verify that delta output can have no newly emitted text while accumulated logprob data exists; in that case the completion’s logprobs are empty for the current delta [tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py:56-78]().

### Public Output Objects

`CompletionOutput` represents one completion sequence. Its fields include generated text and token IDs, cumulative logprob, optional per-token logprobs, finish and stop reasons, LoRA information, sampling masks, speculative-decoding metrics, and weight-version spans [vllm/outputs.py:58-101]().

`RequestOutput` represents the request-level result and carries prompt information, prompt logprobs, one or more completion outputs, a finished flag, and optional metrics and cache or transfer metadata [vllm/outputs.py:137-181]().

`RequestError` represents a request-level error that does not mark the engine unhealthy. Its `to_exception` method maps validation errors, retryable errors, and other generation errors to their respective exception types [vllm/outputs.py:22-35]().

### Engine Output to Request Output

Diagram: Engine output processing and response construction
```mermaid
graph LR
    EngineCoreOutput["EngineCoreOutput"] --> OutputProcessor["OutputProcessor"]
    OutputProcessor --> RequestState["RequestState"]
    RequestState --> IncrementalDetokenizer["IncrementalDetokenizer"]
    RequestState --> LogprobsProcessor["LogprobsProcessor"]
    OutputProcessor --> RequestOutput["RequestOutput"]
    RequestOutput --> CompletionOutput["CompletionOutput"]
```

`OutputProcessor`’s module imports engine output types, `IncrementalDetokenizer`, and `LogprobsProcessor`; `RequestState` accepts the detokenizer and logprobs processor as constructor inputs [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:14-44](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:183-197](). The public completion and request output types are defined in `vllm/outputs.py` [vllm/outputs.py:58-181]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:14-197](), [tests/v1/engine/test_output_processor.py:56-179](), [vllm/outputs.py:22-181]()

## Logprobs Processing and Representation

The output path uses `LogprobsProcessor` as request-local state, while the worker-to-engine output structures represent logprobs as tensors or NumPy arrays before they are converted into public response data [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-35](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:183-197]().

`LogprobsTensors` carries token IDs, logprob values, selected token ranks, and optional generated-token boundaries [vllm/v1/outputs.py:89-128](). Its conversion methods can copy the data to CPU non-blockingly and produce a `LogprobsLists` representation.

`LogprobsLists` stores the corresponding arrays and can slice the flattened data for one request and a requested number of positions [vllm/v1/outputs.py:34-57]().

At the public output layer, `CompletionOutput.logprobs` carries optional sample logprobs, while `RequestOutput.prompt_logprobs` carries optional prompt logprobs [vllm/outputs.py:58-92](), [vllm/outputs.py:137-152]().

### Logprobs Data Flow

Diagram: Worker logprob data to public completion output
```mermaid
graph LR
    SamplerOutput["SamplerOutput"] --> AsyncOutput["AsyncOutput"]
    AsyncOutput --> LogprobsTensors["LogprobsTensors"]
    LogprobsTensors --> LogprobsLists["LogprobsLists"]
    LogprobsLists --> LogprobsProcessor["LogprobsProcessor"]
    LogprobsProcessor --> CompletionOutput["CompletionOutput"]
```

`AsyncOutput` copies sample logprobs to CPU when present. `LogprobsTensors` supplies conversion to `LogprobsLists`, and the output processor imports `LogprobsProcessor` for request-local processing [vllm/v1/outputs.py:34-128](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-35]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-197](), [vllm/v1/outputs.py:34-128](), [vllm/outputs.py:58-152]()

---

## Streaming Response Generation

`RequestOutputCollector` buffers outputs for an individual request and hands them to an asyncio consumer [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:53-93](). Its `put` operation is non-blocking; `get` waits for an output, clears the stored value, and raises it if the stored value is an exception.

For delta output, the collector enables aggregation. When a producer gets ahead of the consumer, successive `RequestOutput` instances are merged using `RequestOutput.add`, with the aggregation behavior selected by the output kind [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:61-84](). Pooling outputs replace the stored pooling output.

`StreamingInputOutputCollector` specializes collection for streaming-input requests [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:129-160](). It maintains a backlog and avoids merging across input-chunk boundaries, identified by a completion finishing while the overall request remains unfinished [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:117-148]().

Collectors can cancel an associated input-stream task when closed; their finalizer also schedules cancellation if the collector is discarded while a task remains attached [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:106-115]().

### Streaming Data Flow

Diagram: Per-request output buffering and async consumption
```mermaid
graph LR
    OutputProcessor["OutputProcessor"] --> RequestOutputCollector["RequestOutputCollector"]
    RequestOutputCollector --> AsyncConsumer["AsyncConsumer"]
    RequestOutputCollector --> MergedOutput["MergedOutput"]
    RequestOutputCollector --> StreamingCollector["StreamingInputOutputCollector"]
    StreamingCollector --> Backlog["Backlog"]
    AsyncConsumer --> ClientResult["ClientResult"]
```

The collector exposes non-blocking `put`, waiting and non-blocking retrieval methods, and a readiness event [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:53-105](). Its streaming-input subclass uses a backlog to retain outputs across chunk boundaries [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:129-160]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:53-160]()

## Summary

`InputProcessor` binds configuration, validation, multimodal budgeting, and a renderer into the request-preparation path [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:170-172](). Renderers provide tokenization and multimodal processing support, with `HfRenderer` handling chat utilities and prompt-embedding placeholder expansion [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-172]().

On output, request-local state connects incremental detokenization and logprob processing to completion results [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-44](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:183-197](). `RequestOutputCollector` provides asynchronous buffering, with delta aggregation and a chunk-aware variant for streaming-input requests [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:53-160]().

Sources: [vllm/renderers/base.py:106-172](), [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:170-172](), [vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py:32-197](), [vllm/outputs.py:58-181]()

## Purpose and scope

This page describes the observability interfaces visible in the provided code: engine statistics and logger initialization, tracing setup, profiling interfaces, and the Prometheus lifecycle hooks. It focuses on how the engine-facing code connects to those interfaces; details of individual metric definitions and exporter implementations are not included in the supplied file contents. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:70-76](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:43-46]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:70-76](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:43-46]()

---

## Architecture Overview

The engine-facing observability path has two distinct parts:

- **Statistics:** `AsyncLLM` and `LLMEngine` reference `IterationStats` and initialize a `StatLoggerManager` when logging is enabled. The async engine also enables logging when custom logger factories are present, even if `log_stats=False`. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:155-165](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:126-134]()
- **Tracing and profiling:** Both engine wrappers initialize a tracer when `observability_config.otlp_traces_endpoint` is set. The engine client protocol exposes tracing status and profiling operations. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:147-151](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:71-75](), [vllm/engine/protocol.py:157-180]()

The sources provided do not show the metric definitions, logger implementations, scrape route, or the engine-step code that creates and forwards each statistics object. The diagram therefore depicts the observable connections supported by the supplied code, rather than an exhaustive metrics data path.

## StatLoggerManager Initialization

`AsyncLLM` accepts `stat_loggers`, combines them with factories returned by `load_stat_logger_plugin_factories()`, and enables stats logging when either `log_stats` is true or at least one custom factory is found. If custom loggers exist while `log_stats=False`, it logs that custom logging is enabled without default stat loggers. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:96-110](), [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:155-165]()

`LLMEngine` accepts optional `stat_loggers` and creates a `StatLoggerManager` when `self.log_stats` is true. It passes the config, custom loggers, default-logger setting, and aggregation setting to the manager, then calls `log_engine_initialized()`. The supplied excerpt does not show the manager’s internal logger selection or record/log scheduling. [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:57-67](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:126-134]()

| Engine-facing symbol | Role shown in the supplied code |
|---|---|
| `StatLoggerFactory` | Type used for custom logger factories accepted by the engine wrappers. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:70-73](), [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:43-45]() |
| `load_stat_logger_plugin_factories()` | Supplies additional factories in `AsyncLLM`. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:155-157]() |
| `StatLoggerManager` | Manager initialized by `LLMEngine` when stats logging is enabled. [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:126-134]() |
| `log_engine_initialized()` | Initialization notification issued by `LLMEngine` to the manager. [vllm/v1/engine/llm_engine.py:126-134]() |

## Profiling Interfaces

The `EngineClient` protocol exposes `start_profile()` and `stop_profile()`. `start_profile()` accepts an optional profile prefix and per-session overrides for delay and maximum iterations. [vllm/engine/protocol.py:168-181]()

`AsyncLLM` imports `TorchProfilerWrapper` and `create_frontend_profiler`, and accepts an optional profiler wrapper in its initializer. `EngineCoreClient` also exposes a `profile()` method with start/stop, prefix, delay, and iteration-bound parameters. The supplied excerpts show these interfaces, not the profiler implementation or the data format and destination of generated profiles. [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:43-46](), [vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:96-110](), [vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py:187-194]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page provides a high-level overview of GPU model execution in vLLM, detailing how worker-side execution connects scheduled batches to model computation, KV cache management, speculative decoding, and generation outputs. It introduces `GPUModelRunner`, `Worker`, and the main execution stages, then links to child pages for implementation details. The stable runner file explicitly aims to keep shared logic minimal and move model-specific behavior into dedicated modules [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-16]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-16]()

## Architecture Overview

GPU execution sits between the engine’s scheduling decisions and the hardware-accelerated model computation. The runner prepares batch inputs and execution metadata, coordinates the forward pass and related cache work, and returns model outputs. Worker and executor coordination layers manage device setup, process boundaries, and parallelism. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:10-17]()

## 4.1. GPUModelRunner

`GPUModelRunner` serves as the primary coordination point for a GPU execution step. It manages input batching, attention metadata construction, forward pass execution, KV cache interaction, and sampling [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-16](). The V1 model runner implementation maintains a stable, minimal core shared across generative, embedding, text, and multimodal models.

For deep-dive coverage of forward passes, model states, CUDA graph management via `CudaGraphManager` and `BatchExecutionDescriptor`, block tables, and pooling or multimodal subcomponents, see the dedicated child page.

For details, see [GPUModelRunner](#4.1).

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-16](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:75-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:154-164]()

## 4.2. Worker and Executor Architecture

The `Worker` class provides the device-level context for execution, handling GPU memory profiling, allocator configuration, and weight initialization [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner.py:73-76](). It coordinates with Executor classes (such as multiproc and Ray executors) to distribute model execution across multiple devices and nodes.

Worker initialization, device lifecycle management, and executor topologies are documented extensively in the child page.

For details, see [Worker and Executor Architecture](#4.2).

Sources: [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner.py:73-76]()

## 4.3. InputBatch and Request State Management

`InputBatch` encapsulates the batched execution state for a single model step. It aggregates request identifiers, token IDs, sequence lengths, tensor indices (`idx_mapping`), and query location markers (`query_start_loc`) [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-116](). Reusable device tensors are managed via `InputBuffers` to avoid allocation overhead during active serving [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:23-40]().

For detailed explanations of `CachedRequestState`, block table indexing, and batched state updates across execution iterations, see the child page.

For details, see [InputBatch and Request State Management](#4.3).

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:23-40](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-116]()

## 4.4. Sampling and Token Generation

Token generation concludes each model forward pass through the `Sampler` module and logits-processing utilities [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:159-162](). This subsystem handles constraints, logprobs computation, temperature scaling, top-k/top-p filtering, and penalty applications.

For comprehensive documentation on `SamplingParams`, logits processors, structured output masking, and token selection strategies, see the child page.

For details, see [Sampling and Token Generation](#4.4).

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:159-162]()

## 4.5. Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding integrates proposal and verification mechanisms into the execution pipeline. Speculators such as `BaseSpeculator`, `DraftModelSpeculator`, `AutoRegressiveSpeculator`, and `TargetDependentARSpeculator` propose speculative tokens using draft models, N-gram matching, or multi-token prediction (MTP) heads [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:67-145](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/autoregressive/speculator.py:24-25](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/target_dependent_ar/speculator.py:23-28]().

For detailed coverage of draft token management, rejection sampling estimators, and acceptance metrics, see the child page.

For details, see [Speculative Decoding](#4.5).

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:67-145](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/autoregressive/speculator.py:24-25](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/target_dependent_ar/speculator.py:23-28]()

## 4.6. Determinism and Batch Invariance

To guarantee stable outputs and reproducible execution, vLLM supports batch-invariant kernels and deterministic operating modes. Execution descriptors (`BatchExecutionDescriptor`) enforce shape consistency across captures and replays [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:75-90]().

For documentation on batch-invariant kernels, deterministic execution flags, and the determinism test suite, see the child page.

For details, see [Determinism and Batch Invariance](#4.6).

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:75-90]()

### GPU Model Execution Pipeline Overview

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SchedulerOutput["SchedulerOutput"] --> InputBatch["InputBatch"]
    InputBatch --> PrepareInputs["Prepare inputs"]
    PrepareInputs --> AttnMeta["Attention metadata & KV cache"]
    AttnMeta --> ModelForward["Model forward"]
    ModelForward --> LogitsProc["Logits processing"]
    LogitsProc --> Sampler["Sampler"]
    Sampler --> SpecDecode["Optional speculative proposal & verification"]
    SpecDecode --> ModelRunnerOutput["ModelRunnerOutput"]
```

This pipeline links scheduling outputs (`SchedulerOutput`) to batch formatting (`InputBatch`), execution dispatch, model forward computation, and final token generation (`ModelRunnerOutput`) [vllm/v1/core/sched/output.py:77-77](), [vllm/v1/outputs.py:87-88](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-116]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/core/sched/output.py:77-77](), [vllm/v1/outputs.py:87-88](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-116]()

## Summary

GPU execution bridges engine-level scheduling with hardware-accelerated tensor computations. `InputBatch` provides structural request state, while `GPUModelRunner` orchestrates the forward pass, KV cache layout, sampling, and speculative execution. Detailed architectural breakdowns are maintained in the respective child pages.

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-16](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-116]()

## Purpose and Scope

`GPUModelRunner` coordinates GPU-side model execution: preparing batches, invoking model-forward and attention infrastructure, managing KV-cache-related state, and routing outputs into sampling or pooling paths. The V1 GPU runner imports dedicated components for these responsibilities, including `InputBatch`, `BlockTables`, `Sampler`, `PoolingRunner`, model-state initialization, and CUDA-graph management [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-155]().

This page covers the stable runner and Model Runner V2, their execution-state interfaces, batch and block-table data flow, CUDA-graph descriptors, and sampling, pooling, multimodal, and speculative-decoding components [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1-17]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1-17](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-155]()

## Architecture and Core Components

The V2 runner is located in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py`. Its module-level style guide notes that the runner is shared across text and multimodal, generative and embedding, public and private models, directing model-specific behavior to model-specific files and keeping the shared path minimal [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:3-17]().

The imports expose principal subsystems: batch preparation and request state, attention and KV cache setup, CUDA graphs, sampling, pooling, multimodal encoder caching, pipeline parallel handling, and speculative decoding [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-177]().

## Request Lifecycle and State Management

`InputBuffers` allocates device tensors for input IDs, positions, padding flags, query start locations, sequence lengths, and DCP local sequence lengths [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:23-40](). `InputBatch` encapsulates batched requests, index mappings, scheduled token counts, query start locations, sequence lengths, and logit indices [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-106]().

`InputBatch.make_dummy` constructs dummy batch instances for graph capture and warmup using `InputBuffers` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:135-142]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:23-40](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:43-106](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:135-142]()

`CudaGraphManager` captures and dispatches CUDA graphs for the model runner [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:154-180](). `BatchExecutionDescriptor` describes batch shapes and CUDA graph modes to ensure shape matches between capture and runtime [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:74-90]().

## KV Cache and Block Tables

`BlockTables` manages block allocation tables, staged writes, and slot mappings across multiple KV cache groups [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96](). It supports context parallelism parameters (`cp_size`, `cp_rank`, `cp_interleave`) and utilizes `FusedStagedWriter` for multi-group updates [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:28-82]().

`BlockTables.append_block_ids` stages new block IDs for requests, and `BlockTables.apply_staged_writes` commits them to device memory [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-158]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-158]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page describes how vLLM’s v1 executors coordinate worker initialization and execution, and how the GPU `Worker` participates in device setup and memory profiling. ## Architecture Overview

An executor acts as the coordination bridge between the engine-side control plane and the worker-side model execution plane. `UniProcExecutor` hosts a `WorkerWrapperBase` directly in the local process, whereas `MultiprocExecutor` spawns worker subprocesses and coordinates them using shared memory message queues (`MessageQueue`). [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:23-27](), [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-75](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:31-33](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:70-73]()

### Executor and Worker Code Entities

This diagram bridges natural language concepts to concrete code entities within the vLLM codebase (`UniProcExecutor`, `MultiprocExecutor`, `WorkerWrapperBase`, `Worker`, `MessageQueue`).

**Executor topology and code entities**

```mermaid
graph TD
  Engine["EngineCoreClient"] --> Executor["Executor (Abstract base)"]
  Executor --> Uni["UniProcExecutor"]
  Executor --> Multi["MultiprocExecutor"]
  Executor --> RayV2["RayExecutorV2"]
  Uni --> Wrapper["WorkerWrapperBase"]
  Wrapper --> Worker["Worker"]
  Multi --> MQ["MessageQueue"]
  Multi --> Proc["BaseProcess / OMPProcessManager"]
  Proc --> Worker
  RayV2 --> RayHandles["ray_worker_handles"]
  RayV2 --> ResponseMQs["response_mqs"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:23-27](), [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-75](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:31-33](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:70-73](), [tests/distributed/test_ray_v2_executor.py:80-103]()

### GPU Worker Responsibilities

The `Worker` class (defined in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py`) inherits from `WorkerBase` and coordinates device initialization, memory profiling, model loading, weight updates, and execution via `GPUModelRunner` or `GPUModelRunnerV2`. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:105-125](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:157-185]()

## Executor Coordination

### `UniProcExecutor`

`UniProcExecutor` (defined in `vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py`) instantiates a local `WorkerWrapperBase` with `rpc_rank=0`. It establishes distributed environment parameters via `_distributed_args()`, configures local network device environment variables (`set_worker_net_device`), and invokes `init_worker()` and `init_device()`. [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-69]()

```python
# Conceptual initialization snippet from UniProcExecutor._init_executor
self.driver_worker = WorkerWrapperBase(rpc_rank=0)
distributed_init_method, rank, local_rank = self._distributed_args()
kwargs = dict(
    vllm_config=self.vllm_config,
    local_rank=local_rank,
    rank=rank,
    distributed_init_method=distributed_init_method,
    is_driver_worker=True,
    shared_worker_lock=Lock(),
)
self.driver_worker.init_worker(all_kwargs=[kwargs])
self.driver_worker.init_device()
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-75]()

`collective_rpc()` dispatches method calls to `driver_worker` using `run_method()`. In non-blocking mode, it returns an `AsyncOutputFuture` if the output is an `AsyncModelRunnerOutput`, allowing asynchronous evaluation. [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:90-117]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:90-117]()

### `MultiprocExecutor`

`MultiprocExecutor` (defined in `vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py`) manages multi-process tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism. It validates that `world_size` matches the product of tensor, pipeline, and prefill-context parallel sizes (`tp_size * pp_size * pcp_size`), sets up multiprocessing environments, and coordinates message queues for scheduler outputs. [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:111-177]()

**Multiprocess initialization: visible coordination path**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as "MultiprocExecutor"
  participant C as "_get_parallel_sizes"
  participant MQ as "MessageQueue"
  participant P as "get_mp_context"
  participant L as "Lock"

  E->>E: "_init_executor installs shutdown finalizer"
  E->>C: "validate world_size == tp_size * pp_size * pcp_size"
  E->>E: "compute num_local_procs and set_multiprocessing_worker_envs"
  E->>MQ: "create leader MessageQueue when node rank is 0"
  E->>MQ: "export scheduler_output_handle"
  E->>P: "get_mp_context()"
  E->>L: "initialize shared worker Lock"
  E->>E: "spawn worker processes"
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:118-177]()

### Uniproc Execution Data Flow

This diagram associates natural language operations with specific methods like `UniProcExecutor.collective_rpc`, `run_method`, and `WorkerWrapperBase`.

**`UniProcExecutor` RPC and execution path**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Caller as "EngineCore"
  participant U as "UniProcExecutor"
  participant R as "run_method"
  participant W as "WorkerWrapperBase"
  participant O as "AsyncModelRunnerOutput"

  Caller->>U: "execute_model(scheduler_output)"
  U->>U: "collective_rpc('execute_model', single_value=True)"
  U->>R: "run_method(driver_worker, method, args, kwargs)"
  R->>W: "invoke worker execute_model()"
  W-->>U: "ModelRunnerOutput or AsyncModelRunnerOutput"
  alt "non-blocking async output"
    U-->>Caller: "AsyncOutputFuture"
    Caller->>O: "result() calls get_output()"
  else "blocking call"

  end
```

## Ray Executors

### `RayExecutorV2`

`RayExecutorV2` initializes distributed workers across Ray nodes. Integration tests establish that `RayExecutorV2` is created when `distributed_executor_backend="ray"`, exposing properties like `ray_worker_handles`, `response_mqs`, and worker ranks. When pipeline parallelism (`pp_size > 1`) is active, it validates `max_concurrent_batches` against pipeline constraints. [tests/distributed/test_ray_v2_executor.py:32-53](), [tests/distributed/test_ray_v2_executor.py:80-107]()

## GPU Worker Initialization and Device Management

The GPU worker (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py`) initializes PyTorch device bindings, sets random seeds, sets up distributed communication groups (`ensure_model_parallel_initialized`), and loads model weights using `get_model_loader()`. It also supports startup plans (`maybe_apply_startup_plan`, `maybe_save_startup_plan`) to speed up worker initialization. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:27-32](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:69-76](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:105-125]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:27-32](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:69-76](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:105-125]()

---

## Memory Profiling and KV Cache Sizing

GPU memory profiling determines the maximum available memory for the KV cache block pool. The worker uses `MemorySnapshot` and `memory_profiling` to measure baseline consumption and peak memory during a dummy forward pass or sizing warmup. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:89-98](), [vllm/utils/mem_utils.py:127-190]()

On ROCm platforms where free memory measurements can fluctuate, `maybe_rocm_profiling_fallback()` provides a fallback based on process-local PyTorch-reserved memory delta when total consumption is negative. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:152-176]()

**ROCm profiling fallback decision**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Start["MemoryProfilingResult"] --> Check["total_consumed >= 0 or current_platform.is_rocm()?"]
  Check -->|"yes"| None["return None"]
  Check -->|"no"| Baseline["read before_create MemorySnapshot"]
  Baseline --> After["read after_profile MemorySnapshot"]
  After --> Reserved["compute non-negative Torch reserved delta"]
  Reserved --> Return["return torch_reserved memory bytes"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:152-176](), [vllm/utils/mem_utils.py:127-190]()

---

## Weight Transfer Delegation

The GPU worker delegates weight updates and layer reloading to a configured `WeightTransferEngine` (created via `WeightTransferEngineFactory`). During an active update session (`start_weight_update()`, `update_weights()`, `finish_weight_update()`), the worker ensures proper state handling and resets LoRA states upon completion. [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker_weight_transfer.py:3-8](), [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker_weight_transfer.py:127-195]()

Sources: [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker_weight_transfer.py:3-8](), [tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker_weight_transfer.py:127-195](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:59-65]()

---

## Summary

`UniProcExecutor` coordinates a single in-process worker via `WorkerWrapperBase`, while `MultiprocExecutor` handles multi-process synchronization and message queue initialization. The GPU `Worker` manages distributed environments, executes memory profiling for KV cache allocation, and delegates weight transfers to specialized engines. [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-75](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:118-177](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:105-125]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/executor/uniproc_executor.py:51-75](), [vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py:118-177](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:105-125]()

## Purpose and scope

This page explains the request and batch data structures used by the V1 GPU worker, how per-request state relates to the batch prepared for execution, and how KV block-table and execution-shape concerns fit into that flow. The primary focus is `CachedRequestState` and `InputBatch` in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py`; the distinct GPU-runner batch representation in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py` is also covered where its fields are visible. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124]()

## Core data structures

### `CachedRequestState`

`CachedRequestState` stores persistent metadata for an individual request. Its fields include request identity, prompt and output token data, multimodal features, sampling and pooling parameters, KV block IDs, computed-token progress, and optional request-specific state such as prompt embeddings, LoRA metadata, and prompt-logprob accumulation. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-63]()

On initialization, `__post_init__` derives `num_prompt_tokens` from the available prompt token IDs or prompt embeddings. If pooling parameters are present, it initializes `pooling_states`. The `num_tokens` property returns prompt length plus output-token count. `get_token_id` reads from prompt IDs or generated output IDs; if a requested prompt position was supplied only as embeddings, it raises an error because that token ID is unknown. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:65-87]()

| Field or helper | Role |
|---|---|
| `req_id` | Request identifier. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-36]() |
| `prompt_token_ids`, `prompt_embeds`, `mm_features` | Prompt content and multimodal input metadata. Prompt content can be represented by token IDs or embeddings. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:36-47]() |
| `output_token_ids`, `num_computed_tokens` | Generated output history and computed-token progress. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:42-44]() |
| `block_ids` | Per-group KV block IDs, represented as a tuple of integer lists. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:42-44]() |
| `sampling_params`, `generator` | Sampling configuration and optional PyTorch generator. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:38-40]() |
| `mrope_positions`, `mrope_position_delta` | Optional request-level positional state. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:46-47]() |
| `lora_request`, `in_progress_prompt_logprobs_cpu` | Optional adapter state and accumulated prompt-logprob chunks. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:49-52]() |
| `prompt_is_token_ids`, `prev_num_draft_len` | Mixed token/embedding prompt mask and speculative-decoding-related state. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:54-59]() |
| `pooling_params`, `pooling_states` | Optional pooling configuration and runtime state. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:61-63]() |
| `num_prompt_tokens`, `num_tokens`, `get_token_id` | Derived prompt length, total request length, and token lookup helpers. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:65-87]() |

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-87]()

### `InputBatch`: request-oriented batch storage

The `InputBatch` in `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py` is a long-lived, capacity-bounded container for request-indexed state. It is initialized with limits such as `max_num_reqs`, `max_model_len`, and `max_num_batched_tokens`, as well as device, vocabulary, KV block-size, and optional feature configuration. It maintains request IDs and an ID-to-index map. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-125]()

The visible initialization code creates CPU-side storage for token IDs and token-versus-embedding flags, a dictionary for prompt embeddings keyed by request index, and arrays/tensors for token counts and computed-token counts. The token and mask tensors are CPU-resident; prompt embeddings are stored per request rather than in one maximum-sized prompt-embedding allocation. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:127-169]()

| Storage | Shape or mapping | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `_req_ids`, `req_id_to_index` | Request-indexed list and ID-to-index dictionary. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:124-125]() | Associate request IDs with batch slots. |
| `token_ids_cpu_tensor`, `is_token_ids_tensor` | `(max_num_reqs, max_model_len)`. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:131-144]() | Store CPU token values and identify positions represented by token IDs. |
| `req_prompt_embeds` | `req_index -> tensor`. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:145-148]() | Keep prompt embeddings on a per-request basis. |
| `num_tokens_no_spec`, `num_prompt_tokens`, `num_computed_tokens_cpu` | Per-request arrays backed by CPU tensors. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:149-169]() | Track request token counts and computed-token progress. |

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-169]()

### `InputBatch`: GPU execution-step representation

`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py` defines another `InputBatch` with a different role: it describes a particular execution batch. It contains the scheduled request IDs and counts, maps batch positions to request-state indices, tracks scheduled tokens and token totals, and carries per-step sequence and query metadata. Its fields also include token inputs, positions, padding flags, logits indices, and flags for structured-output and prefill/decode handling. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124]()

`InputBuffers` owns reusable device buffers for token IDs, positions, padding flags, query-start locations, sequence lengths, and DCP-local sequence lengths. `InputBatch.make_dummy` constructs a dummy batch using those buffers; the visible implementation creates synthetic request IDs and sets up a token distribution and sequence/query metadata for the requested dummy shape. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:19-35](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:126-172]()

This distinction matters when reading call sites: `GPUModelRunner` imports `InputBatch`, `InputBuffers`, and batch-preparation helpers from `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.input_batch`, while the `CachedRequestState` definition and request-oriented `InputBatch` are in `vllm.v1.worker.gpu_input_batch`. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:19-35](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:126-172](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130]()

### From request state to execution batch

The following diagram links the request-level concepts to the code entities that represent them using precise class and module identifiers.

**Diagram: Request state and GPU execution batch code entities**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Request["RequestMetadata"] --> CRS["CachedRequestState"]
    CRS --> RequestBatch["InputBatchInGpuInputBatchPy"]
    RequestBatch --> TokenStore["token_ids_cpu_tensor"]
    RequestBatch --> EmbedStore["req_prompt_embeds"]
    RequestBatch --> IndexMap["req_id_to_index"]
    Runner["GPUModelRunner"] --> StepBatch["InputBatchInGpuInputBatchModule"]
    StepBatch --> StepBuffers["InputBuffers"]
    StepBatch --> QueryMeta["query_start_loc"]
    StepBatch --> TokenInputs["input_ids"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-169](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:19-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130]()

## Block tables and KV-cache indexing

### Block-table relationship to request and batch state

The request-oriented `CachedRequestState.block_ids` records KV block IDs as a tuple of lists, with the tuple structure allowing multiple KV cache groups. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:42-44]() The GPU execution code imports `BlockTables` from `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py`, and attention utilities expose `build_slot_mappings_by_layer`, which is imported by the model runner and used in the attention utility layer. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-105]()

The `BlockTables` class manages block tables for multiple KV cache groups. It stores `block_tables` as a list of `StagedWriteTensor` objects, one for each KV cache group. Each `StagedWriteTensor` holds a GPU tensor of shape `(max_num_reqs, max_num_blocks)`. `num_blocks` tracks the number of blocks used per request per group. `slot_mappings` is a tensor used to map token positions to KV cache slots. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96]()

`append_block_ids` stages writes to the block tables for a given request. It updates the `StagedWriteTensor` for each KV cache group and increments `num_blocks`. `apply_staged_writes` then commits these staged writes to the GPU. If there's only one KV cache group, it calls `apply_write` directly on the `StagedWriteTensor`. For multiple groups, it uses a `FusedStagedWriter` to apply all writes in a single fused kernel. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-159]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:42-44](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-105](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-159]()

### Block tables in context/parallel execution

`PCPManager` describes a flow in which the runner keeps the global scheduled batch while the manager rewrites a per-step `InputBatch` into rank-local rows, retaining a global-batch view for restoration before sampling and postprocessing. It can attach `BlockTables`; when tables are present, it creates local table tensors corresponding to the input block tables and allocates global and gathered slot-mapping buffers per KV-cache group. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:38-45](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:94-139]()

This shows why block tables and batch indexing must be considered together: the per-step request layout may be transformed for local execution, while the block-table and slot-mapping data must be available in compatible global or local shapes. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:69-76](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:94-139]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:38-45](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:69-76](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:94-139]()

## GPUModelRunner and batched execution state

`GPUModelRunner` imports the execution-step `InputBatch` and `InputBuffers` together with helpers for token combination, index mapping, post-update processing, position/sequence-length preparation, prefill preparation, and dummy context setup. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130]()

The execution-step batch carries both host-side scheduling facts and device tensors needed for a forward pass. Its fields distinguish scheduled-token counts and total token counts from padded counts, and include `query_start_loc`, `seq_lens`, token positions, padding markers, and logits-selection metadata. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-99]()

**Diagram: Scheduled-batch concepts mapped to execution code**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Scheduler["SchedulerOutput"] --> Runner["GPUModelRunner"]
    Runner --> Helpers["prepare_prefill_inputs"]
    Helpers --> Batch["InputBatch"]
    Batch --> QueryStarts["query_start_loc"]
    Batch --> SeqLens["seq_lens"]
    Batch --> TokenData["input_ids"]
    Batch --> Logits["logits_indices"]
    Batch --> Padding["is_padding"]
    Batch --> Forward["ModelForward"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-99]()

### Batch shape and CUDA graph descriptors

`BatchExecutionDescriptor` records execution shape and CUDA graph mode, including token count, optional request count, optional uniform token count, optional maximum query length, active LoRA count, and microbatch count. Its documentation describes matching runtime shapes to captured graph shapes. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:70-86]()

The compatibility check allows a descriptor to match only when its configured shape constraints accommodate the runtime request/token counts and other tracked dimensions. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:111-138]()

`InputBatch.make_dummy` supplies synthetic batch metadata for a requested number of requests and tokens, distributing tokens across dummy requests and populating sequence lengths and query-start locations. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:126-172]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:70-86](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:111-138](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:126-172]()

### Model-specific request state

`ModelState` provides hooks for adding and removing request-specific model state, applying staged writes, initializing KV cache, preprocessing state before a forward pass, and postprocessing state. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/interface.py:121-173]()

`DefaultModelState` implements request handling for optional RoPE and prompt-embedding state. On request addition it initializes prefill positions when RoPE state exists and adds prompt-embedding state when enabled; on removal it forwards the removal to prompt-embedding state. During input preparation it reads the execution batch’s unpadded token IDs and can prepare embeddings from model token embeddings or multimodal embeddings. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:67-92](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:100-133]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/interface.py:121-173](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:67-92](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:100-133]()

## CPU and device buffer organization

`InputBuffers` allocates device-resident reusable tensors for token IDs, positions, padding flags, query-start locations, sequence lengths, and DCP-local sequence lengths. The corresponding `InputBatch` stores views or references to the active portions of those buffers alongside batch counts and CPU-side NumPy metadata. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:19-35](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:65-99]()

The request-oriented `InputBatch` has a different storage pattern: token IDs and mixed-input flags are CPU tensors with NumPy views, while per-request prompt embeddings are held in a dictionary. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:127-169]()

`StagedWriteTensor` is a utility class for efficiently writing data from CPU to GPU. It stages writes in CPU memory and then applies them to a GPU tensor. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/buffer_utils.py:150-189]()

**Diagram: Separate storage layers**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Persistent["CachedRequestState"] --> RequestStorage["InputBatch"]
    RequestStorage --> CpuTokens["token_ids_cpu_tensor"]
    RequestStorage --> MixedMask["is_token_ids_tensor"]
    RequestStorage --> PromptEmbeds["req_prompt_embeds"]
    RequestStorage --> Progress["num_computed_tokens_cpu_tensor"]
    StepStorage["InputBuffers"] --> DeviceTokens["input_ids"]
    StepStorage --> DevicePositions["positions"]
    StepStorage --> DeviceSeqLens["seq_lens"]
    StepStorage --> QueryOffsets["query_start_loc"]
    DeviceTokens --> StepBatch["InputBatch"]
    DevicePositions --> StepBatch
    DeviceSeqLens --> StepBatch
    QueryOffsets --> StepBatch
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:127-169](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:19-35](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:65-99](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/buffer_utils.py:150-189]()

## Prompt tokens, embeddings, and multimodal inputs

The request-level representation supports prompt token IDs, prompt embeddings, and multimodal feature specifications. `CachedRequestState` calculates prompt length from token IDs or embeddings; `get_token_id` can return token IDs only when those IDs exist for the requested prompt position. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:36-47](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:65-87]()

The request-oriented `InputBatch` stores token-ID values and a per-position boolean mask indicating whether prompt positions are token IDs, while keeping prompt-embedding tensors in `req_prompt_embeds`. The default model state prepares the execution batch’s inputs using unpadded token IDs; for multimodal models it executes scheduled encoder inputs and gathers multimodal embeddings before producing model embeddings. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:131-148](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:100-133]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:36-47](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:65-87](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:131-148](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_states/default.py:100-133]()

## Reasoning and speculative-decoding state

The request-oriented `InputBatch` can initialize a thinking-budget state holder when a `ReasoningConfig` is supplied, and tracks request IDs associated with thinking-token budgets. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-116]()

`ThinkingBudgetStateHolder` tracks thinking sections within requests and forces end tokens when a budget is exceeded. It maintains per-request state including `in_think` status, `think_count`, and `countdown`. `sync_batch` manages the lifecycle of per-request state, and `apply_to_logits` masks and adjusts logits to enforce thinking budget constraints. [vllm/v1/sample/thinking_budget_state.py:34-160]()

Speculative-decoding interfaces consume the GPU execution batch directly: `BaseSpeculator.propose` accepts an `InputBatch` together with attention metadata, slot mappings, hidden states, and sampled/rejected counts. `DraftModelSpeculator` allocates its own `InputBuffers` using the configured maximum request and token capacities. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:61-103](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:106-154]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-116](), [vllm/v1/sample/thinking_budget_state.py:34-160](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:61-103](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:106-154]()

## Summary

`CachedRequestState` represents persistent per-request information, including prompt and output content, block IDs, token progress, and optional model features. The request-oriented `InputBatch` stores request-indexed CPU metadata and prompt embeddings; the GPU execution-step `InputBatch` represents scheduled rows, token inputs, sequence metadata, logits indices, and padding state. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-169](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:120-130]()

`BlockTables` and slot-mapping utilities connect request block assignments to attention execution, managing staged writes and fused updates to GPU block tables. `PCPManager` additionally maintains local block-table and slot-mapping buffers for context-parallel batch transformations. CUDA graph shape matching uses `BatchExecutionDescriptor` to represent the runtime dimensions relevant to replay compatibility. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:42-44](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-105](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-159](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:94-139](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:70-86]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:34-90](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu_input_batch.py:90-169](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/input_batch.py:38-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:98-130](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:17-96](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/block_table.py:125-159](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:94-139](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py:70-86]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page describes the V1 GPU sampling path: how the worker’s `Sampler` registers per-request sampling state, prepares logits processors, selects a platform-appropriate top-k/top-p implementation, and exposes logprob-related state. It also covers structured-output parameters, grammar-backed backends (`XgrammarBackend`, `OutlinesBackend`, and `GuidanceBackend`), and the engine-level managers that prepare grammar constraints and apply token bitmasks. [vllm/sampling_params.py:101-141](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:33-122](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:38-161](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_outlines.py:39-88]()

Sources: [vllm/sampling_params.py:101-141](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:33-122](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:38-161](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_outlines.py:39-88]()

## Sampling Components and Architecture

The GPU worker’s `Sampler` coordinates request-specific sampling state and logits processors. At construction, it creates sampling states, penalties state, logit bias state, bad words state, logprob token IDs state, and thinking budget state. It builds an ordered `logits_processors` list containing logit bias, penalties, bad-word filtering, and any supplied custom processors. The order is intentional because bias addition and penalty scaling are not commutative operations [vllm/sampling_params.py:94-141]().

`SamplingType` distinguishes greedy, random, and seeded-random modes. `StructuredOutputsParams` represents one structured-output constraint—JSON, regex, choice, grammar, JSON-object mode, or structural tag—and validates that exactly one constraint is provided [vllm/sampling_params.py:101-141]().

### Sampling Pipeline — Natural Language to Code Mapping

The diagram links user-facing generation concepts to code entities present in the codebase. Structured-output processing is managed via backends like `XgrammarBackend` and `OutlinesBackend` using constraints defined in `StructuredOutputsParams`. [vllm/sampling_params.py:101-141](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:38-161](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_outlines.py:39-88](), [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_sampler.py:103-164]()

## Sampling Parameters and State Management

### `SamplingParams` and Related Parameter Types

`SamplingParams` configures generation behavior per request. 

The primary parameter types include:

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `SamplingType` | Enumerates `GREEDY` (0), `RANDOM` (1), and `RANDOM_SEED` (2). [vllm/sampling_params.py:94-98]() |
| `StructuredOutputsParams` | Holds one structured-output constraint plus options such as whitespace controls and structural tags. Post-init validation requires exactly one constraint field to be non-null. [vllm/sampling_params.py:101-141]() |
| `RepetitionDetectionParams` | Holds N-gram repetition-detection limits, including maximum and minimum pattern sizes and a minimum repetition count. [vllm/sampling_params.py:172-188]() |

`MAX_LOGPROB_TOKEN_IDS` is an upper bound on the length of `SamplingParams.logprob_token_ids`, matching the row width allocated by the sampler's `LogprobTokenIdsState` [vllm/sampling_params.py:35-37]().

Sources: [vllm/sampling_params.py:35-37](), [vllm/sampling_params.py:94-141](), [vllm/sampling_params.py:172-188]()

## Logits Processors: Penalties, Biases, and Filters

Processors apply modifications to output logits prior to token selection. These include logit biases, repetition/presence penalties, bad word masks, and custom user-defined logits processors. Execution order is strictly enforced: logit biases are applied first, followed by penalties, and then bad-word filters, ensuring deterministic composition. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:81-82]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:81-82]()

## Structured Output Masking and Grammar Guidance

`StructuredOutputsParams` accepts a single constraint from JSON, regex, choice, grammar, JSON-object mode, or structural tag. Post-init validation rejects requests with multiple constraint kinds or with none [vllm/sampling_params.py:122-141]().

### Structured Output Backends

vLLM supports multiple grammar and structured-output compiler backends:
- **`XgrammarBackend`**: Compiles JSON schemas or grammars using `xgrammar` [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:38-161](). It handles special tokens by maintaining separate compilers for JSON (disallowing special tokens) and structural tags (allowing special tokens) [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_xgrammar.py:104-112]().
- **`OutlinesBackend`**: Builds regexes from JSON schemas or direct patterns via `outlines_core` and compiles token index guides [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_outlines.py:39-88]().
- **`GuidanceBackend`**: Uses `llguidance` for token-level grammar guidance and structural matching [vllm/v1/structured_output/backend_guidance.py:132-195]().

### Structured Output Pipeline Mapping

This diagram maps a schema constraint from its request parameter to structured output compilation backends and bitmask application routines. ### Grammar Bitmask Alignment and Speculative Padding

`apply_grammar_bitmask` receives scheduler output, grammar output, input batch, and logits, reordering the compact grammar bitmask to match the GPU batch request order while accounting for scheduled speculative tokens [vllm/v1/structured_output/utils.py:101-164]().

`strip_speculative_padding` removes negative sentinel padding from token ID lists prior to grammar validation [vllm/v1/structured_output/utils.py:48-59]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/structured_output/utils.py:48-59](), [vllm/v1/structured_output/utils.py:101-164]()

## Token Selection and Logprobs Computation

### Top-k/Top-p Implementations and Kernel Dispatch

Token selection uses accelerator-specific kernels or PyTorch fallbacks:
- **FlashInfer Sampler**: `flashinfer_sampler_supported` checks CUDA platform compatibility, enablement via `VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER`, compute capability, and device SM counts (>16 SMs required) [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_sampler.py:103-164]().
- **XPU Sampler**: Checked via `xpu_sampler_supported` for Intel XPU hardware [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_sampler.py:167-175]().
- **Triton Kernels**: Combined top-k/top-p Triton kernels (`_topk_topp_kernel`) implement pivot-based truncation and selection based on Qrita algorithms [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py:83-149]().

### Prompt and Sample Logprobs Workers

`PromptLogprobsWorker` computes logprobs for prompt tokens across prefill chunks [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:33-122](). It gathers token IDs, applies mask checks, and computes token logprobs or raw logits depending on `logprobs_mode` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:81-120]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_sampler.py:103-175](), [vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py:83-149](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/prompt_logprob.py:33-120]()

## Purpose and Scope

Speculative decoding lets a target model verify token proposals made by a drafter, so a decoding step can produce more than one output token when proposals are accepted. This page describes the proposer and verifier roles, the methods identifiable in the codebase (including `ngram`, draft models, `eagle`, `dflash`, `dspark`, `medusa`/`MTP`, and suffix decoding), draft token and probability data management, rejection sampling mechanics, and acceptance metrics. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:111-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:50-70]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:111-124](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:50-70]()

---

## Architecture Overview

A proposer prepares draft tokens or draft-model inputs; the target model supplies logits; and `RejectionSampler` combines target logits, optional draft probabilities, speculative metadata, and sampling metadata to produce final output token IDs. `draft_probs` may be absent for `ngram` speculation, while target logits are flattened across requests. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:125-156]()

Proposer-specific execution paths include:
- `DraftModelSpeculator` (which `EagleSpeculator` and `DFlashSpeculator` inherit from) passes hidden states to its model [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:12-18]().
- `DFlashSpeculator` and `DSparkSpeculator` construct specialized parallel query and multi-token inputs [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/speculator.py:3-28]().

### Speculative Decoding Data Flow

**Diagram: proposer inputs, target verification, and sampled output**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["DraftModelSpeculator"] -->|"draft tokens or model inputs"| B["Target model forward"]
    B -->|"target logits"| C["RejectionSampler.forward"]
    A -->|"draft_probs, optional"| C
    D["SpecDecodeMetadata"] --> C
    E["SamplingMetadata"] --> C
    C -->|"SamplerOutput: token IDs and optional logprobs"| F["Next decoding step"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:125-156]()

### Natural-Language Roles Mapped to Code Entities

**Diagram: speculative decoding roles and the code entities that implement them**

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    C["Prepare parallel query inputs"] --> D["DFlashSpeculator"]
    E["Load and align a DSpark draft model"] --> F["load_dspark_model"]
    G["Verify proposals and form output tokens"] --> H["RejectionSampler"]
    B --> I["TargetDependentARSpeculator"]
    D --> I
    H --> J["SamplerOutput"]
```

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/eagle/speculator.py:12-18](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash/speculator.py:38-55](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/utils.py:72-122](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:147-156]()

## Speculative Methods

Supported speculator types and registration mechanisms are located in configuration and transformer utility modules [vllm/transformers_utils/configs/speculators/algos.py:7-12]():

| Method or family | Code-backed description |
|---|---|
| `ngram` | `RejectionSampler.forward` allows `draft_probs=None` for ngram speculative decoding. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:125-140]() |
| `draft_model` | Standard autonomous draft model execution utilizing `DraftModelSpeculator`. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:12-18]() |
| `eagle` / `eagle3` / `peagle` | `EagleSpeculator` passes auxiliary hidden states from target layers to the drafter. Configuration transformations handle `eagle3` and `peagle` speculator variants [vllm/transformers_utils/configs/speculators/algos.py:15-88](). |
| `dflash` / `dflash2` | `DFlashSpeculator` handles parallel drafting with mask tokens and target intermediate hidden states (`aux_hidden_state_layer_ids`) [vllm/transformers_utils/configs/speculators/algos.py:90-148](). |
| `dspark` | Semi-autoregressive parallel drafting with a lightweight sequential Markov head, batch-sharded sampling, and custom attention backends [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/speculator.py:3-28](). |
| Medusa / MTP | Multi-token prediction (MTP) heads (such as DeepSeek MTP layers) recycle post-final-norm hidden states across draft steps [vllm/models/deepseek_v32/nvidia/mtp.py:64-101](), [vllm/model_executor/models/deepseek_mtp.py:76-112](). |
| Suffix decoding | Suffix lookup proposer architectures integrated via the base framework. |

Sources: [vllm/transformers_utils/configs/speculators/algos.py:7-148](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dspark/speculator.py:3-28](), [vllm/models/deepseek_v32/nvidia/mtp.py:64-101]()

---

## Rejection Sampling and Verification

`RejectionSampler` combines a `Sampler`, speculative configurations, and metadata to verify draft tokens against target logits [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:147-162](). 

### Accepted, Recovered, and Bonus Tokens

The verification pass classifies tokens into:
- **Accepted**: Draft tokens that successfully pass the probability ratio test against target logits [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:58-101]().
- **Recovered**: Tokens sampled from the residual probability distribution when a draft token is rejected [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:58-101]().
- **Bonus**: Target-sampled tokens appended when all proposed draft tokens are accepted [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:50-70]().

### Probability Normalization and Gumbel Sampling

Log-sum-exp reductions and residual mass calculations are executed via Triton kernels in `rejection_sampler_utils.py` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:20-101](). Randomness for speculative sampling uses Gumbel-max noise generation with distinct noise salts for drafts and targets to ensure proper coupling and verification consistency [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/gumbel.py:15-19](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/gumbel.py:170-199]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:147-162](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:20-101](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/sample/gumbel.py:15-19]()

---

## Acceptance Metrics and Verification Modes

`RejectionSampler` supports multiple verification strategies configured via `SpeculativeConfig`:
- **Synthetic Mode**: Converts unconditional acceptance rates to conditional rates using `unconditional_to_conditional_rates` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:168-176]().
- **Block Verification**: Enabled via `rejection_sample_method == "block"` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:177-178]().
- **FLy Entropy-based Verification**: Dynamic window verification controlled by `fly_window_size`, `fly_entropy_threshold`, and `fly_entropy_top_k` [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:164-166]().

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:161-182]()

---

**Diagram: method names and searchable implementation symbols**

```mermaid

    A["EAGLE hidden-state drafting"] --> B["EagleSpeculator"]
    B --> C["TargetDependentARSpeculator"]
    D["DFlash parallel query preparation"] --> E["DFlashSpeculator"]
    F["DSpark draft model setup"] --> G["load_dspark_model"]
```

## Summary

Speculative decoding in vLLM is structured around modular proposers (`EagleSpeculator`, `DFlashSpeculator`, `DSparkSpeculator`) that feed draft distributions or hidden states into the target model, which are subsequently validated by `RejectionSampler` using Triton-accelerated rejection kernels and Gumbel sampling strategies. [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:12-18](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:147-162](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:20-101]()

Sources: [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py:12-18](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler.py:147-162](), [vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/rejection_sampler_utils.py:20-101]()

## Purpose and scope

This page describes vLLM’s batch-invariance mode, the deterministic execution measures documented for it, the visible Triton and custom kernel implementations (including persistent matmul, RMSNorm, LoRA shrink, and custom all-reduce), tuned matmul configuration structures, and the determinism test suite shown in `tests/v1/determinism/`. Batch invariance aims to make a request’s output independent of the batch size and request order. It is currently documented as beta. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:3-7]()

Sources: `docs/features/batch_invariance.md:3-7`()

---

## 1. Motivation and core concepts

Batch invariance addresses numerical differences that can arise when inference runs with different batch sizes or request order. The feature is intended to support framework and model debugging, reproducible reinforcement-learning rollouts, and large-scale inference validation. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:9-16]()

The feature’s stated goal is deterministic model output across batch sizes and request order. Tests in this area check several levels of that goal: generated text or token IDs, per-step log probabilities, and individual kernel outputs. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:7]()[tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py:32-45]()

Sources: `docs/features/batch_invariance.md:7-16`, `tests/v1/determinism/test_batch_invariance.py:32-45`

---

## 2. Enabling and hardware prerequisites

### Hardware and attention backend requirements

The feature documentation lists NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or higher, AMD Instinct GPUs in the `gfx90a`, `gfx942`, and `gfx950` families, and Intel XPUs with Triton support. On XPU, the documented requirement is to select the Triton attention backend, `TRITON_ATTN`. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:18-29]()

The determinism test utility independently builds an available-backend list: CUDA devices with capability 8.0 or higher use `FLASH_ATTN`, `TRITON_ATTN`, and `FLEX_ATTENTION`; XPU with Triton and ROCm with Triton use `TRITON_ATTN`. It marks tests as skipped when no supported device is available. [tests/v1/determinism/utils.py:24-41]()[tests/v1/determinism/utils.py:64-82]()

### Activation

Set `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` to enable batch invariance. The feature documentation gives both server-mode and offline-inference examples. For seeded generation, the examples also set a sampling seed, such as `seed=42`. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:45-50]()[docs/features/batch_invariance.md:53-82]()[docs/features/batch_invariance.md:84-120]()

### Execution behavior documented for the mode

The feature documentation lists these execution changes when batch invariance is enabled:

| Area | Documented behavior |
|---|---|
| Kernels | Use deterministic implementations for attention and other operations, aiming for consistent numerical behavior across batch sizes. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:152-156]() |
| Tensor-parallel all-reduce | Keep custom all-reduce enabled with a fixed reduction order; pin the one-stage kernel and reduce large inputs in fixed-size chunks (`vllm/distributed/device_communicators/custom_all_reduce.py` sets `batch_invariant = envs.VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`). Disable FlashInfer, AITER, and QuickReduce all-reduce. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:157]()[vllm/distributed/device_communicators/custom_all_reduce.py:185]() |
| CUDA matmul and graphs | On CUDA devices with tuned matmul entries for the model’s bf16 unquantized forward linear layers (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell), run without `torch.compile` using breakable CUDA graphs so tile configurations follow runtime batch size; `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=0` opts out. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:158-159]() |
| LoRA shrink | Divide the shrink reduction into 8 fixed K chunks (`_BI_SPLIT_K = 8`) and sum them in a fixed order rather than using atomics. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:160]()[vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py:22-23]() |

The documentation warns that tensor-parallel batch invariance is not supported for all-reduces whose size is not a multiple of 16 bytes. Such tensors can switch between NCCL and custom all-reduce depending on batch size; the documentation gives hidden sizes not divisible by 8 in fp16/bf16 as an example. [docs/features/batch_invariance.md:162-163]()

### Natural-language-to-code map: enablement and test backend selection

**Diagram: User-facing settings mapped to implementation and test entities**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    User["EnableBatchInvariantInference"] --> Env["VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1"]
    User --> XPU["SelectXPUTritonAttention"]
    XPU --> AttnConfig["attention_config.backend = TRITON_ATTN"]
    Env --> BI["vllm.model_executor.determinism.batch_invariant"]
    BI --> Matmul["matmul_kernel_persistent"]
    BI --> RMS["rms_norm_batch_invariant"]
    Tests["DeterminismTestSelection"] --> Utils["tests/v1/determinism/utils.py"]
    Utils --> Backends["BACKENDS"]
    Backends --> CUDA["CUDA: FLASH_ATTN, TRITON_ATTN, FLEX_ATTENTION"]
    Backends --> XPUBackend["XPU: TRITON_ATTN"]
    Backends --> ROCm["ROCm: TRITON_ATTN"]
```

## 3. Batch-invariant kernel implementation

The implementation in `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py` and related modules provides Triton persistent matmul kernels, RMSNorm implementations, LoRA shrink reduction chunks, and deterministic custom all-reduce routines. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:3-22]()[vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py:22-23]()[csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:7-23]()

### Persistent matmul kernels

`matmul_kernel_persistent` assigns program IDs to tiles and iterates over tile IDs with a stride of `NUM_SMS`. For each output tile, it iterates through K tiles in order, accumulates with `tl.dot`, optionally adds bias, converts to the output element type, and stores the result. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:48-137]()

`matmul_kernel_descriptor_persistent` is a tensor-descriptor-based persistent matmul. Its documented input convention is a transposed B matrix with shape `[N, K]` and K-contiguous row-major layout; it creates descriptors for A, B, and C. The file describes this kernel as using 2D block I/O and notes a performance benefit on Intel XPU. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:140-190]()

The helper `_compute_pid` maps a tile ID to M and N program IDs using grouped tile scheduling. Both visible persistent kernels use it to determine tile coordinates. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:38-45]()[vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:80-88]()[vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:121-124]()

### Tuned configuration data structures

`batch_invariant_configs.py` defines `_MatmulMConfig` with `block_m`, `block_n`, `num_warps`, and `num_stages`, and `_MatmulShapeConfig` with `block_k` and `m_buckets`. `_BATCH_INVARIANT_MATMUL_TUNED_CONFIGS` stores configuration data by architecture family and matrix shape; the shown entries include Ada and Hopper. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:11-25]()[vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:26-103]()

| Entity | Role |
|---|---|
| `_MatmulMConfig` | Holds tile dimensions and launch parameters. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:11-16]() |
| `_MatmulShapeConfig` | Holds the K tile size and M-bucket configurations. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:18-21]() |
| `_BATCH_INVARIANT_MATMUL_TUNED_CONFIGS` | Maps architecture family and matrix shape to tuned shape configuration. [vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:23-25]() |

### Custom All-Reduce and LoRA Shrink Kernels

In `csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh`, `cross_device_reduce_1stage` implements deterministic reduction order by ensuring addresses are not reordered across ranks:
```cpp
template <typename T, int ngpus>
__global__ void __launch_bounds__(512, 1)
    cross_device_reduce_1stage(RankData* _dp, RankSignals sg, Signal* self_sg,
                               T* __restrict__ result, int rank, int size) {
  // note: we don't reorder the address so the accumulation order is the same
  // for all ranks, ensuring bitwise identical results
  ...
}
```
[csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:7-15]()

For LoRA layers, `_lora_shrink_reduce_kernel` in `vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py` splits $K$ into `_BI_SPLIT_K = 8` fixed partial chunks, avoiding non-deterministic atomic updates across varying batch sizes [vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py:22-23]()[vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py:26-98]().

### Natural-language-to-code map: matmul configuration and kernel path

**Diagram: Tuned shape configuration mapped to persistent kernel entities**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Shape["ModelLinearLayerShape"] --> Arch["ArchitectureFamily"]
    Arch --> Configs["_BATCH_INVARIANT_MATMUL_TUNED_CONFIGS"]
    Configs --> ShapeConfig["_MatmulShapeConfig"]
    ShapeConfig --> Buckets["m_buckets"]
    Buckets --> MConfig["_MatmulMConfig"]
    MConfig --> Launch["PersistentMatmulLaunchParameters"]
    Launch --> PointerKernel["matmul_kernel_persistent"]
    Launch --> DescriptorKernel["matmul_kernel_descriptor_persistent"]
    PointerKernel --> Output["CTileStore"]
    DescriptorKernel --> Output
```

Sources: `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:11-25`, `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant_configs.py:26-103`, `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:38-49`, `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:80-137`, `vllm/model_executor/determinism/batch_invariant.py:140-190`, `csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:7-23`, `vllm/lora/ops/triton_ops/lora_shrink_op.py:22-98`
